newsitem.title: USA: FORECAST - US Sept production growth may moderate.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - US Sept production growth may moderate.

text.p: U.S. industrial production probably continued to grow in September, despite weaker-than -expected manufacturing data in the latest U.S. employment report, analysts said.
Some economists surveyed by Reuters have even given their production forecasts a longer-term bias to the upside, citing recent information from the country's purchasing managers.
The average forecast in the Reuters survey said the report by the Federal Reserve on Thursday at 0915 EDT/1315 GMT should show a 0.1 percent rise in industrial production in September.
The survey also forecast a moderation in capacity utilization to 83.3 from 83.5.
Industrial production rose 0.5 percent in August following a 0.1 percent increase in July, the Fed said.
Forecasts were pushed lower in the wake of weak manufacturing employment numbers in September, according to Rosanne Cahn, vice president and economist at CS First Boston Corp.
In the latest report from the U.S. Labor Department, September factory jobs fell by 57,000, while construction and retail rose by 9,000 and 22,000 jobs, respectively.

But other economists warned the payrolls report gives only a snapshot of production, and expected little interruption in the moderate growth rate. For instance, economists at MCM MoneyWatch Inc and Yamaichi International (America) Inc expect gains of 0.3 percent and 0.4 percent, respectively.

Beyond payrolls influence, Cahn said the overall pace of production remains healthy. She noted that purchasing managers reported new orders in the 55 to 56 range for August and September. That would translate into a five to six percent annualized rate of growth, she said.
"The purchasing managers survey indicates that the manufacturing sector continues to be pretty strong when you step back from monthly volatility and the government data," Cahn said.

Michael Niemira, economist at Bank of Tokyo-Mitsubishi Ltd, expected a slight decline in production for September but said a rebuilding of inventories should keep the statistic on an upward trend through the fourth quarter.
"If you look at the inventory growth numbers against the orders it suggests there is still room for inventory rebuilding ..." Niemira said.
"If businesses have confidence in the economy beyond the near-term I don't think there's any reason not to expect a strengthening," Niemira added.
Niemira expects a 0.3 to 0.4 percent growth range for the near-term as inventories mount. That number should then retreat to reflect a growth rate of 0.2 percent, he said.

MCM MoneyWatch senior economist Astrid Adolfson said she expects inventory rebuilding to complement production based on better chain-store sales, consumer confidence and the upcoming gift-giving season.

Niemira said weakness in utilities and mining should drag the number lower, but they are two components that "may be less meaningful to the economy." Moderation in the automotive sector may also factor into a softer number, he said.

Adolfson said auto production is up from month to month, however, and will add substance to September's production number. Looking ahead, she said General Motors cutbacks due to a strike in Canada will likely depress production in the future.
